utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, we are Thursday, the 12th of June, 2008. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, as well as the Registrar, the usher, and all the people assisting us in this courtroom. We have a witness who is about to enter the courtroom. I believe that Mr. Mundis would like to say something. But before that, I would like to remind Mr. Mundis of the fact that the Trial Chamber has asked him to give us an updated list of all the witnesses that you are going to call based on your 65 ter list. We need this list, and I personally need this list also because I need to see whether or not we need to take some time off the Prosecution's time, given that some witnesses have stated that they wish to be Defence witnesses. So this may have an impact on your time allocation. I need to have this list as soon as possible. I know that this takes a lot of time, you need to check some of the data, but I had asked to have this months ago already. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and to Dr. Seselj and everyone in and around the courtroom. With respect to the request, I will endeavour to have that to the Trial Chamber by Tuesday of next week. I will, as I've indicated before, state that the Prosecution position is that notwithstanding the fact that some of the witnesses have indicated that they would prefer to be Defence witnesses, that, in and of itself, is not sufficient reasons for the Prosecution to remove those names and that the list that we will be providing is substantially the same list that has been filed earlier with the Trial Chamber. But I will provide an updated list that obviously no longer contains the names of those witnesses who have already testified. As Your Honours are aware, several weeks ago, following some discussions on the issue and the providing of a lengthy list to Dr. Seselj, he specifically requested the disclosure of a large amount of video material in the Prosecution's possession. This video material excludes suspect interviews or any other taped interviews of any witnesses or suspects. I do have today with me in the courtroom 11 hard drives -- 11 hard drives containing approximately 3.000 gigabytes of data. This represents approximately 6.600 hours of video material. We are in a position to disclose that to Dr. Seselj today. I understand, from a logistical point of view, that there may be some issues with the Detention Unit concerning this material. It's in five boxes on a trolley immediately behind me. Before disclosing this, however, the Prosecution would respectfully request a specific order from the Trial Chamber directing Dr. Seselj, number one, to return all of this material, these hard drives, to the Office of the Prosecutor upon the completion of these proceedings. That's point 1. We would also ask for an order directing Dr. Seselj not to copy this video material and, number three, a specific order directing Dr. Seselj not to disclose this material to anyone who is not associated with his Defence team. I also feel duty-bound to place on the record the fact that the overwhelming bulk of this video material was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by commercial broadcasting companies and, therefore, is subject to applicable copyright with respect to this material. Our view is that the only, and I stress "only" legitimate use for this material by the accused is for the preparation of his case. I point this out because there are indications that Dr. Seselj in the past has published some of the witness statements taken by OTP that have been disclosed to him, and some of these statements have been published in his books. And in our respectful submission, in light of the purpose for which this material -- this video material is being disclosed, and because it is subject to various property rights by the commercial broadcasters who provided it to the Office of the Prosecutor for purposes of investigation and use at trial, it would be inappropriate, in our view, for Dr. Seselj to use this material for any other purpose; for example, creation of documentaries or other broadcasts or rebroadcasts of this material simply on the grounds that it was provided to him by the OTP. That is not, in our respectful view, an appropriate use for this material, and we would specifically ask the Trial Chamber to issue an order to the effect that, again, this material needs to be returned, that it is not to be copied, and it is not to be disclosed or in any other way broadcast or turned into commercial documentaries, or commercial films, or in any other way rebroadcast. So we would ask for an order from the Trial Chamber to that effect, and we believe that that is a prudent course of action, given the history of some of the other material that has been disclosed to Dr. Seselj and which has subsequently worked its way into the public domain as a result of publishing and other steps taken by Dr. Seselj. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two questions of a technical nature to put to you, Mr. Mundis. The first question is this: If these copies are given to Mr. Seselj, can he forward them to his associates in Belgrade, according to you, so that they can watch these videos, which represent 6.000 hours of viewing time? Mr. Seselj, of course, can't view these images for 6.000 hours. No individual can view these images for 6.000 hours. So as he can't do it himself, from a technical point of view, he will give us his point of view, but I anticipate this. I'm just asking you whether according to what you have just told us, he is entitled -- if the Trial Chamber were to grant this, if he is entitled to transmit this or disclose this material to his associates. That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The answer to that is "yes." As I indicated before, it would be a legitimate use of this material for Dr. Seselj and members of his team to review this material. And, again, we fully understand the amount of time. That was one reason why we produced a multi-hundred-page spreadsheet of this information. And you will recall Dr. Seselj said he wanted all of it. It is a huge amount of material. It is in an electronic format that would allow it to be watched by way of computers. The earlier spreadsheet that we gave him, which again was, I believe, 700 or 800 -- more than a thousand pages, provides detailed information about what's contained on the videos that are on the hard drives. But it's a simple question of using a cable, just like any other external hard drive, plugging it into the computer, and by way of various media players that are installed on computers, viewing the material. It would certainly be a legitimate use for his associates to review the material. It would not, in our respectful view, be a legitimate purpose or use of this material if it were to be rebroadcast or turned into movies, or documentaries, or anything of that nature, for the simple reason that the material is subject to copyright laws and was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by commercial broadcasting entities for purposes of use in investigative purposes or at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second question now, which is partly illustrated by your previous answer. You have a spreadsheet which represents some thousand pages, in which you have given a list of all the videos contained in these images so you can follow. Now, at the OTP I'm sure you have received videos from different sources, some videos which were in the public domain and other videos which were of a private nature, and you quite rightly mentioned this, with property rights, commercial property rights, intellectual property and copyright issues. So let's assume, because I don't have the spreadsheet in front of me so I don't know where these videos come from, but let's assume that a commercial company, let's take the case of the BBC, for instance, that shot a report somewhere, the BBC has rights, has broadcasting rights. Therefore, the BBC can demand of the person who might broadcast some of its images, rights, so this may give rise to a problem. On your spreadsheet, do you have clear references to these videos? Have you indicated which videos are protected by copyright? And the commercial firms that gave you these videos have said to you, "We are prepared to give you these videos if they are not broadcast outside and if you are prepared to pay for the copyright." Strictly speaking, they could not object to these videos being broadcast in the courtroom, but they can have something to say if these images are used in a commercial arena. So my question is a very simple one. On this list you have prepared, have you clearly made a distinction what videos are in the public domain and which videos could give rise to copyright issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a real problem. My colleague has also a question to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I just wanted to ensure that when you hand over the material to the accused, that there is a tool by which it is possible to identify one of the entries in the registry that you are giving into the video. Is it possible, when you sit with your list in front of you and you come across a piece that you want to see, can you then actually go from there and find the relevant spot in the CDs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, each of the various -- each of the 11 hard drives has an index of what is contained on that hard drive, so the overall index that's a thousand pages long, in effect, has been broken up into what is on each of the hard drives. So it is certainly possible to look at the index for what's contained -- which files are on that hard drive and then go to those files on the hard drive based on the ERN number that's set forth on the index and which is the file name, if you will, for each of the various clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you can confirm that it is possible to actually identify the material and find it on the CD-ROMs? Otherwise, 6.000 hours of video is useless, unless you have a very efficient tool to find the pieces you want to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, and this is precisely why the first step of this process was the production of an index that would allow Dr. Seselj to select whatever it is he wanted, and it was his choice -- I stress that it was his choice for all of this material. We're certainly not -- I'm not walking in here and dumping 6.600 hours of video material on an unrepresented accused. This is material he specifically asked for after we produced a detailed index that would allow him to select whatever it is that he wanted, and it was partially because of the fact that he demanded or asked for all of this material that gave rise to our request that this material not form its way or make its way into any commercial broadcasts or any other use of this material that would be improper, in our respectful views. Let me just make one other very brief comment about that use of material. As the Presiding Judge has clearly indicated, some of this material came from sources other than commercial broadcasters, such as a victim or perhaps a witness who had a videotape of something that they handed over to us. That would be subject to property rights in the same way as something that was owned by the BBC, and so the real issue here is that virtually all of this material someone owns the copyrights to, and the fact that it may have been used in a trial here or put into the public domain by way of broadcasting does not mean that it can then be used for commercial purposes by anyone else. And so our view is notwithstanding the fact that there's not a tick box or a specific indication as to each of these videos, our view is the only legitimate use for this material is for purposes of the trial or perhaps for investigative lead purposes. This material is not being disclosed so that Dr. Seselj can branch off into the broadcasting or movie-making industry, following in the wake of his publishing career. That is not, in our view, a responsible or legitimate use of this material. It must be put to some kind of forensic use, and that is the purpose for which it's being disclosed today, and that is why we have specifically asked for an order that would include a provision that the material be returned, that it not be copied, and that it not be disclosed or rebroadcast outside of Dr. Seselj's team, in order to preserve the property rights of the individuals who provided the material to the Tribunal for specific forensic purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know, in B/C/S or in English, the spreadsheet. Is the spreadsheet in B/C/S or in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The spreadsheet is in English, Your Honour. It would take a considerable period of time to translate this spreadsheet into B/C/S. That would simply, in our respectful view, not be a good use of our limited translation resources in order to undertake that kind of process. I will state, however, that because many of the videos relate to names, place names, dates, that it is possible, simply by looking at these spreadsheets, to identify and narrow down what it is exactly that we're looking for. And of course the original spreadsheet was provided in English, and at the time when Dr. Seselj indicated that he would accept these videos, he did indicate on the record that he would accept the videos in their original language. Much of this material, the actual videos themselves, are in B/C/S; not all of them, of course. Many of them are also Western broadcasts that are of a variety of languages, German, French, English, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question. You said that these videos can be made available to Mr. Seselj's associates. I wanted to know whether you mean all Seselj's associates or Mr. Seselj's associates who have a confidentiality status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We would submit that it would be the latter category, Your Honours, those who have the confidentiality status, as Your Honour has put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall now give the floor to Mr. Seselj. As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of justice that in the course of a trial, material is being disclosed which may give rise to copyright issues. Therefore, legally speaking, this is extremely complex. Mr. Seselj, I'm sure, will shed some light on this. Mr. Seselj, what is your position on this? Would you like to file submissions after what's been said? I'll give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like to state my views orally and to round off that question. First of all, I have never published so far or disclosed to the public, put in the public domain, any document that I received from the Prosecutor, the Tribunal, or the Registry which is confidential in nature, and I'm only bound by this -- the confidential nature of the documents if the Registry writes something confidential which relates to my state of health, for example, or my status, or anything like that, with regard to my hunger strike, the financing of my Defence and so on and so forth. Then the Registry can't make it incumbent on me to keep it secret, so that is an abuse on the Registry's part. As a rule, the Trial Chamber can proclaim something to be confidential, and so can the OTP proclaim a document of its own as confidential. Now, I never published any documents like that. In my books, I published exclusively documents from the public domain. Now, as far as the interviews are concerned which the Prosecution conducted with various individuals -- with suspects, that is to say, suspect interviews, I made public those documents if the suspect would bring in -- were to bring in the video himself and then allow us to put that down on paper. Then I did that, and I have the right to do that, because the suspect decides whether he's going to make his interviews accessible to the public or not. You can't conduct a suspect interview and then tell the suspect, "You can't show that to anyone." That's absolutely impossible. And that is how I published the interview with Ljubisa Petkovic, for example, in my book entitled "The Devil's Disciple and the Criminal Pope, John Paul II." I also published certain documents that I came by from third parties, some interview statements and so on and so forth, but that has nothing to do with the relationship between the OTP and me and the Tribunal and me. That is up to my investigators to find as they see fit. Now, the specific question here is this: The Prosecution intends to disclose to me a large quantity of videos, hard drives and so on, and is seeking certain guarantees. First of all, it has asked that these materials be returned after they've been used, and I don't think there's any dispute there. Secondly, they want to ensure that that is not published for commercial purposes. I didn't have that intention at all. I don't engage in making documentary films, at least not so far, and it is not my intention to do so in the future, so the Prosecution can rest assured on that score. And I'm not mad enough to publish something like that and then have to pay copyright and reduce myself to pauper status. Thirdly or fourthly -- I don't know which point I reached, three or four, but I'm going to have to make certain copies of some material that I consider should be used during these proceedings. I'm going to have to set that aside from that bulk of material over there because I can't carry all that bulk. Everything that I intend to use during the Defence case or in my cross-examination of the Prosecution witnesses, I have to copy and prepare. Fourthly or fifthly, whatever point I've reached, the 6.000-odd video hours of material is not something that my associates can look through. I have quite a big team of investigators and other legal advisers who are not registered here. They're also working for me. But it's a vast amount, and I'm going to have to have a whole team looking at it and examining it. But all of them have not directly signed their services to the Registry or anything else, but I'm responsible if they violate any rules and regulations, and they have other things to do. So the OTP is protected on that part. But, anyway, within a reasonable space of time, a lot of people will be needed to get through that whole material, and they will go through it and adhere to the principles of confidentiality as applied. And I think that this is much ado about nothing. It is sufficient for the Prosecution to set out all the specific points for which these materials cannot be used, cannot be copied, et cetera, et cetera, and that's it, and everything shown in the courtroom, in public, will be on my web site, and the Prosecution can't prevent me from doing that. Everything that came out in court is on my internet web site, and I think even yesterday's testimony and the cross-examination, because my web site is the most popular in the world. What can I do about it? That's a fact. So as I say, only the material I use in court will no longer be subject to any copyright and cannot be protected because it is in the public domain and I can make it public, so I think we can stop the discussion there, except that I can't have this material carted 'round with me. They put a flak-jacket on me and all the rest of it, so maybe I can carry it in my teeth. That's the only way I can do that. I can't roll that roller around everywhere, and it should be delivered to me in the detention centre. My advisers will come in at the end of the month, and they will have to transport it to Belgrade, to a safe place, and when the trial is over, say, in ten years' time and all the proceedings are completed, we'll see how we are going to use that. Now, as we're having an extensive procedural debate, I have an issue to bring forward at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I heard you and -- I heard what you said, so when you will have all this, you undertake not to disclose to the outside. I heard you well, but there were two things which you said which surprised me. You said that, "The OTP will give all this to me at the end of the proceedings." Maybe I misunderstood what the Prosecution said, what Mr. Mundis said, but I understood that as soon as we rendered a decision, he would immediately disclose all this material to you; not at the end of the proceedings, but right away, as soon as possible. So this would be disclosed to you as quickly as possible. However, once you're done using it, once the trial is over, you must give all this back to the OTP. But you added something else. You said that 10 years from now, when everything's over, you intend to use all this material, so the issue of copyright is not settled, obviously. Please explain, what do you mean when you said that you're going to use it ten years from now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the interpretation you heard was disastrously bad. It was my understanding that the OTP was offering that to me today, and I said that they should send it to prison rather than having me lug this in my teeth, because I go to prison with my hands tied and handcuffed. Secondly, I said that I take it upon myself to return it to the OTP when the trial is over, and the trial will be over in about ten years, whatever. You see how slowly this has been moving along; 115 witnesses of theirs and 115 witnesses of mine, so that's at least three years to go, and then the appeal, and then a possible review, and who knows how long all of this is going to take, and who knows before what court this trial is going to end if this Tribunal closes down in 2010. So that is what I had said, knowing what would follow afterwards. So I really think that the interpretation you heard is disastrous. I simply cannot understand that that's the way they interpreted it to you, the way you have interpreted it just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand what you meant now. Thank you. We have been seized by this oral motion. We have heard Mr. Seselj's comments, and the Trial Chamber will issue its decision on this. Let's now bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something else you would like to address, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already informed you about that, that I have to bring up a problem. Last week, we were short of time, but the problem, although not that important, is rather important, in my view, after all. After all, you know that you are the only instance that I can address in terms of irregular conditions of my time in custody in the Scheveningen Prison. The problem occurred the week before last. Upon your instructions, upon one of your orders, Ljubisa Petkovic, one of my key Defence witnesses, was arrested. He was brought to the Detention Unit. My group -- we are not in the same group. My group went out for a walk on Friday the week before last. Ljubisa Petkovic appeared at the window. He waved, and I waved back from the yard, and I shouted out to him, "Hang on." Then the head of the prison guard barged in and sent us all back to our cells, not only me, all of them, and he cut our walk short. I have to tell you that at least one hour of walking in the fresh air, and in Serbia and in civilised countries it is two hours, is an inalienable right of detainees and prisoners. Nothing can bring that into question. The fact that I am shouting in the yard does not mean that I should be banned from walking, or because I raised my hands. No one can stop me from walking or prohibit me. It was not only me. There's nine of us in that group, and all of us were sent back to our cells. So that's the way it was on that day. The beginning of the following week, I think it was Monday, yet again we went out for a walk. Ljubisa Petkovic no longer appeared on the window. They probably scared him over there as well. Who knows what they did to him, and I already thought that they had taken him to another part of the building from which you could not see the yard where people walk. All of a sudden, a prison guard in uniform appeared at the window. Usually, once a month they climb up onto the roof to see what the situation is like, so that a helicopter would not land or that somebody would not try to escape from the roof. As I saw him on the roof this time, I shouted to him if there's a ball up on the roof, that he should throw one down. There were football and basketball balls up there from previous years, and then when the inmates are playing ball, sometimes one of the balls ends up on the roof. And he looked around on the roof and he said, "There isn't a single ball here." All of a sudden, the supervisor of the prison guard again rushes into the yard. His name is (redacted). This time, he only interrupts my walk, and he takes me back to the cell for no reason whatsoever. My understanding was that somebody was asking to see me, the doctor, the warden or whoever, and that's why I left. Otherwise, I would not have gone. Next time, I said that I would not walk on my own two feet. He'd have to carry me on his own back. The third problem happened after Ljubisa Petkovic had arrived here, and he arrived practically without anything. And he barely weighs 20 kilograms, he is so light, and I asked the guard who was on duty on my floor to take ten telephone cards to him, and in writing I submitted a request to the warden to have a little bit of money transferred from my bank account to Ljubisa Petkovic's account. Three days later, the telephone cards were returned to me, and the warden sent a letter -- the deputy warden, a certain (redacted), because the warden retired, he said that that was prohibited because all contact between Ljubisa Petkovic and me is prohibited. So what kind of a contact is that? This is not the first time that I helped another inmate to the best of my ability, and it is customary, after all, that prison inmates help each other out in this way. I think that what happened was something truly incredible and that it requires an intervention from the Trial Chamber itself. I must say that as far as the previous warden was concerned, we did have some problems with him, and I would occasionally speak of problems with him, but the communication was rather favourable. There weren't any incidents in prison. The warden knew how to take a stand in the right way, more or less. But since he retired, this (redacted) who has taken over is doing all sorts of things. I really think that things have become unbearable this way. I've talked only about the problems that concern me personally and this one problem that concerns my entire group, and it seems that I was to be blamed for all of it, and that is why everyone was deprived of a walk on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what you said, there is part of it that the Trial Chamber knew already about and another part that is very new to us and that we're just discovering here now. Let's talk about it. The Trial Chamber decided that Mr. Petkovic should not have any contact with you, since Mr. Petkovic as of now is a witness. He was a Court witness, a Chamber witness, and because of this he's not supposed to contact anyone. This is what we had told the administration of UNDU. And you told us that you wanted to give him some money and some telephone cards. That's what you just said. But since you're not supposed to contact this person, giving him money might be a problem. And we were informed of this, actually. I do not know the financial situation of this person. If he has financial problems, he must tell the warden about it, and the warden will tell the Trial Chamber about it. He can call. He is allowed to get money transfers from his family. This is normal, this is possible. However, this question of waving -- you know, making signs and so on, well, this should not have occurred if, at the UNDU, things were designed in such a way that this would not be possible. Obviously, it did happen, it's not very serious, but they decided to adjourn your walks. I don't have much to say about this. It's their own problem at the UNDU, and it's not up to the Trial Chamber to manage your detention arrangements. It's up to -- it's their problem and it's their competence, and I can't say much about this. However, we will ask the warden to explain why there was a contact at one point in time between the two of you. Now, regarding this problem of the ball that ended up on the roof, that's very minor, it's a minor incident, and it's true that it should have been settled easily. What you said is on the transcript now, and the Registrar is made aware of all this in realtime, and he will find a solution. But the Trial Chamber reaffirms that as of now, Mr. Petkovic is not supposed to contact you for any reason whatsoever. So I believe that this explains the situation. I will convey the answer of the prison warden regarding all these issues. We all agree on the fact that in a detention unit, it is best for everyone to work in good cooperation; wardens, inmates and so forth. Now let's bring the witness in the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis -- Mr. Dutertre, the witness doesn't want any protection measures; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do confirm that there is no protective measures required?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this means that the witness can be brought into the room without closing the blinds?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, let's bring him into the courtroom and we will ask him about all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me check whether you hear me in your own language. If you do, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before you take the solemn declaration, I have a few questions to ask. The first one: Before you came, the OTP had asked for protective measures for you, and recently we just heard that you no longer wanted protective measures to be granted. Could you tell us why you had asked for protective measures and why you no longer want them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I wanted to prove before all and before my own people that as far as the statements of mine are concerned and what happened during the war, I wanted to prove things and I wanted to show what justice is, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this is a personal decision. Nobody told you what you were supposed to do; you decided this yourself. You were not threatened and no one exerted any pressure? No one told you, "Do this," or, "Do that"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, have you already testified in front of a court on the facts that -- on the events that occurred in the former Yugoslavia or is it the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time that I'm testifying here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please give me your name, sir, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness. There's too much background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the interpreters did not hear your name, so would you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Sejdic, Safet. I was born in 1969 in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were born in 1969. Could you give us the month and the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a job at the moment? If so, which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At present, I work in the Public Transportation Company. I work on the maintenance of tram lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you some information. Let me tell you that there may be a problem or there may not, but the Prosecutor is going to ask questions to you for two hours and a half, and the accused will also ask questions for two hours and a half, and the Judges will probably have questions, so we won't finish today, which means that we will have to resume on Tuesday, next Tuesday. Is this a problem for you, to stay over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does not constitute a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem; very well. The Prosecutor must have told you this already when he met with you, but I will repeat it anyway. You will answer questions put to you by the Prosecutor, and he will also show you documents. You must answer his questions as accurately as possible so that we can assess your answers. If you do not understand the meaning of a question, ask the Prosecutor to repeat the question and reformulate it. After this stage, the accused on your left, Mr. Seselj, will put questions to you. He is entitled to do this by the procedure, and he will ask questions to check your credibility and also put questions on the evidence that you will have given when answering questions from the Prosecutor, and the accused will have as much time for his questions as the Prosecutor had. The three Judges on the Bench in front of you will also ask some questions from time to time to shed some light on problems or clear some problems. We break for 20 minutes every hour and a half for technical reasons. The tapes -- the video and the audiotapes need to be changed. We started at 9.00. Therefore, the first break is scheduled for 10.30. If at any point in time you don't feel well, you feel uneasy, you want the proceedings to stop, just raise your hand and ask me to stop and to adjourn the hearing for a moment, and we'll do so. If at any moment also you'd like to talk to the Judges, to the Bench, please do so. We are here to -- we're also here to answer any question that a witness may have. But you are now in the hands of justice. You are the witness of justice. You've taken the solemn declaration. This means that now you're no longer going to have any contact with the representatives of the OTP or with the Defence, nor with the Judges, of course. We're not supposed to have any contacts with you. I'm saying this because you'll be staying here over the weekend, because your testimony will resume on Tuesday, but that means that during the weekend you are not supposed to have any contact with anyone, except of course with your relatives. You can talk to your relatives on private matters only, of course. I needed to say all this to make sure that this hearing would run smoothly and serenely. Serenely, I insist on this. Mr. Dutertre, you have the floor and you may start the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will take the floor very serenely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. We've already had some information regarding your identity and your occupation. I will ask you one first question on your general background, if I may use this word. Where did you live in Bosnia-Herzegovina when the war started?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: I lived in the area of Vogosca in Semizovac. Svrake is the name of the village. It is the municipality of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How long had you been living in Svrake?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: For some 20-odd years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How far is Svrake from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: About 12 or 13 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Sejdic, what was the ethnical makeup of Svrake, your village, before the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: It was a pretty village. That is my favourite town. That's where I grew up, that's where I went to school and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I will reformulate my question. Could you tell us what was the ethnical origin of the inhabitants? Were there more Serbs, more Muslims, more Croats? Give us the ethnical makeup of your village, please.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: There were Serbs and Croats and Muslims. There were also some Roma and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us which group was in the majority, if there was one?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, there were more Serbs. It was predominantly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you give us your ethnical background?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: I'm a Roma by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Are you -- what is your religion, please?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Tell us, what is your religion?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you married in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you have any children? If "yes," how many?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: I had a son on the 18th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In 1992, did you have any other children, apart from this son?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: I had a daughter in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any siblings?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many brothers, how many sisters?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: I have three brothers and a sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where did your parents live in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: The village of Svrake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'm done with this first line of questions, and I will now try to give the chronology of what happened to you during the conflict. And after that, I will pick a number of incidents, and we will go into detail regarding these incidents. So first I'll ask you some questions just to have a general idea of what happened to you during the war, and I will go into details later. The first question: What happened early -- at the beginning of the month of April 1992 in your village?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the month of April 1992, Muslim and Serb and other -- how should I put this -- forces started grouping in order to start this war and things like that. However, allegedly they didn't want to have a war there with the Muslims and the Serbs, and they started saying that there should really be no incidents, so they kept meeting up until they actually started three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you mean by "after three days they started;" could you clarify this? I'd like to get back to this idea, namely, what happened to your village. In April 1992, what happened in your village, in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: In 1992, the war began. Serbs from the surrounding places, from the hills, started an attack on Semizovac and the village of Svrake. They fired from all sides. The Muslims did not have that much power to defend themselves or to move any -- organise any forces to defend themselves because they had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you say "this village," you mean your village, the village of Svrake; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you personally have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: For how long did the Muslims in your village resist this attack?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: They resisted for about two days, as much as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: After they put up a resistance, can you tell us where the Muslim men of your village were taken by the attackers?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This type of question is not allowed. The Prosecutor cannot ask where Muslims were taken by Serbs when the resistance was crushed. He can ask what happened when the resistance was crushed. We don't know yet that the Muslims were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once the resistance had ended, can you tell us what the attackers did with the Muslim men of your village?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: The attackers took women and children on one side and men on the other side. They took the men to the Semizovac barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once you were in the Semizovac barracks, what happened then to these men?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Some were taken there, and they asked those men to surrender any weapons if they had been issued with weapons, and when these men surrendered, some threw down their arms, others had no weapons, those who did not have any weapons were left there. Those who had had weapons were taken to other prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What happened to you? Were you with these men in Semizovac, had you stayed in Svrake? What was your fate?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: I took my wife and child and set off towards Semizovac, where the others were going, too, across the bridge. Some of the Serbs knew that I had not been issued with any weapons and that I wasn't involved in that, so I went to Semizovac. There were buses there outside Kulin Dvor, near Kuzman house in Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And then you stayed in Semizovac or did you go elsewhere? What happened?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Two buses were provided to go towards Srednje, carrying women and children and elderly and infirm men and men who had not been issued with any weapons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, those villagers that went out set off for Srednje. Could you tell me, who were the forces who were in charge of Srednje?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: The Serbs were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Page 27 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did the Serbs in Srednje do with you when you got there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: One of their commanders came out and said that men should be separated from women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once that was done, what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: We men saw before that one bus that was riddled with bullets. There was blood all over. The glass was shattered. All the bus was strafed with bullets. It used to be a public transportation bus. When we started coming out, the women and children started crying, and that chief man could not bear to watch that. He said everybody should turn back into the bus and the buses should turn back towards Semizovac, towards the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Just to clarify, you and your family, you went back in the direction of Semizovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: On the return journey in the direction of Semizovac, can you describe to us what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: There were two vehicles of the Serbian Army, Volkswagen Golfs. One was in front, the other one was behind. The two men who were driving the bus were Muslims. That one Muslim veered suddenly towards Korita village. That was Muslim territory and Muslims lived in that village. So he made a sharp turn with the bus towards that village, so that these two buses did not go to Semizovac eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So you managed to slip away, these two cars that were escorting you, and this was under Muslim control. How much time did you spend in Korita, which was under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: I spent about 20 days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And after 20 or so days, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, I was told, since I belonged to an ethnic minority, as a Roma person -- there were also some Muslims and I believe a few Croats, a few. I don't know exactly. They provided joint guard duty to prevent Serbs from coming into that village, but they didn't let me, my brother, or my father to participate in this guard duty because maybe they didn't trust us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I understand that in Korita, seemingly people didn't trust you because you were a Roma. Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They told us that it was quiet and peaceful in Semizovac, that anyone who wanted to go home could go home, and that those who had family in Sarajevo may go there, that it was free passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Just one point I'd like to clarify. Between Semizovac and Svrake, what distance is there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: The distance between Semizovac and Svrake was perhaps five, ten minutes' walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So you were in Korita, and you've told us that the people in Korita told you that things were quiet and peaceful in Semizovac. What did you do then? Did you go to Semizovac, did you go elsewhere, did you go to Sarajevo? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: My father said since he had family in Sarajevo, his father, mother and sisters were there, that we should go to Sarajevo, but we should first go to Semizovac and then on to Sarajevo, if possible. However, when we came close to Semizovac, when we reached the point of the former post office and near Kuzman's house, we stopped. We were approached by Mr. Nebojsa Spiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'd just like to go back a little. When you say that you went to Semizovac, can you tell us who precisely accompanied you? Who were you with?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Me, my father, my mother, two brothers, my sister, my wife and child.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And then we understand that in April, your village got attacked, resistance was put up for three days, and then you went to Semizovac and then on to Korita, where you stayed for 20 days. So when you returned to Semizovac and when you see Mr. Nebojsa Spiric, what time period is this? Is this the month of May, end of May, beginning of June? Can you tell us this, please?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly the date, but it was 20 days after the beginning of the attack on Svrake, when they drove us away to Srednje and when we arrived at Korita village, so it was 20 days after all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You mentioned that on the return journey, you met Nebojsa Spiric. Who is Nebojsa Spiric? Let me begin by a precise question. What ethnicity is he?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who was he with, if he was with anyone? Maybe he was alone, but if he was with anyone, who was with him?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: He was standing there with Miro Kuzman. He was standing, and he saw us coming; me, my father, my mother, my brother and sister. He approached us and he recognised my brother. And knowing that my brother had been in the Territorial Defence on the Muslim side, and when they were capturing Svrake village my brother had been in the Territorial Defence on the Muslim side, he had been issued a weapon by the Territorial Defence, and they recognised him as one of those who was standing on the bridge outside Svrake to prevent Serbs from coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Having recognised your brother as someone who had guarded the Svrake bridge, what did Mr. Spiric do?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spiric approached and told my father and my mother that my brother should follow him and that after questioning he would be released to go home, that they shouldn't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And did Mr. Spiric in fact detain your brother --

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: He took my brother, interrogated him for a while. He told us to go home. We said we wanted to go to Sarajevo. He said it wasn't possible, "You have to go home. Nobody will do you any harm. I guarantee that." But we had known Spiric from before the war. He was one of the local Serbs. We knew him as one of the neighbours. Even before the war, he was active. He threw his weight about. He liked to get into brawls and fights. He was something like a local gangster.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: We shall get back to details concerning Mr. Spiric later on. I'm just trying to provide you with an outline for the moment. If I understood you correctly, you then go back home with your family. You go back to Svrake; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, to Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Can you clarify this for us, please. Your house is in Svrake or Semizovac, or is it one of your relatives who has a house in Semizovac? I understood to begin with that your house was in Svrake. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in my old grandfather's house. I lived in Svrake with my wife and child, whereas my father had a house on the crossroads in Semizovac. It was like a municipal flat. He had two rooms, a bathroom and a hallway. And during the attack on Svrake, my father joined me in my house, because over there -- sorry. In Svrake, most of our Muslim population was there, more than in Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You've just said -- maybe I misunderstood you. You've just said that you returned, after having seen Mr. Spiric, to Semizovac. You also had a house in Semizovac; is that what I should understand? Could you specify this, please?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: It was my father's house, that flat that I just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Did you see Mr. Spiric again on that day after he had taken your brother away?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where did you see him again?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: When we set off towards our home, on the crossroads in Semizovac there was a police station, a public security station from before the war, and in that police station in Semizovac, that's where Spiric took him. But some of the Serbs, like police, started beating him up. We watched that, and we came up to Spiric and said, "Please don't beat him, don't touch him." He told us to go home quietly, that nothing would happen to my brother, that he will release him later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So did you go back home then?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once you were home, did you see Mr. Spiric again on that day?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: He told us not to leave our home, and later he told to -- he came to tell us about my brother, that he was in detention, that nothing would happen to him. My parents started crying. We all started crying. We told him, "Please, Mr. Spiric, don't let any harm come to him. He is innocent. We are all innocent." He said, "Don't worry, no one will lay a finger on you, and stay in your home."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Apart from that, what did Mr. Spiric tell you? Did he give you any instructions? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: He just said that my brother was in prison in Vogosca and that nothing bad would happen to him. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did any other Serbs come to your house on that day?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, no one, only Spiric who came to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to jog the witness's memory, if possible. This relates to a particular topic. This refers to the 92 ter interview. In English, this is on page 12, in paragraph 49, and I would like to read this out now. Let me start: [In English] " ... on the first day, we are back in Semizovac. Later on, while Spiric was still at our house, Novo Divljanovic and Mico Colakovic came and took us to Semizovac to do our first work for the Serbs." [Interpretation] Is this what you stated, and is this what happened, Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to emphasise that later, when Spiric left, Novo Divljanovic came and told us that we had to go to sweep the streets of Semizovac, that we were going to be something like a labour platoon, doing work for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did you do? What did this work consist of?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, we cleaned the rubbish in Semizovac. We cleaned some of the premises where their troops were to be accommodated. We took out the rubbish from the bunkers. There was one bunker down there. Then we cleaned one of their coffee bars where they gathered. We swept the streets in Svrake around the building of the local commune. There was a shop; we cleaned that as well. We removed the rubbish containers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How long did you do this job for? How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: It was a one or two days' job.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And you continued doing this afterwards? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that, we went on to clean their yards, their gardens, their fields where they were supposed to do the sowing, we chopped wood. And then they took us to be part of a labour platoon digging trenches, preparing defence lines, and we remained in that labour platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You said that you cut some wood and cleaned up the fields, and then after that you were asked to go and dig trenches. Can you tell us when you started digging the trenches? Let me rephrase it the other way 'round. For how long were you involved in domestic chores, and when did you actually start digging the trenches?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: There was not much time. We did that for one or two days, and then they took us to the lines from Njavocici [phoen] village near Vranjak. They took us up there when they captured a certain a line. They wanted to form a base there from which to prevent Muslims from attacking. They held that line up there and they took us there to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: For how many months, years, did you have to do this type of work along the frontlines?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: From that day on, we did that throughout the war. Wherever some work needed to be done, we had to go there and stay there and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you give us a day or a year, to be more precise? How long did you stay in these work patrols?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, from that day in 1992, when it all started, it went on all the way. Until 1994, I was in that labour platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: After 1994, where were you assigned to, what did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Then I went with Mr. Rajko Jankovic, when he was the commander of the frontline and commander of the Semizovac Battalion. I had to accompany him and carry ammunition, food and water for his Intervention Platoon. And during their actions and attacks on Muslim trenches, I had to pull out the wounded and carry them to safety, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to refresh the witness's memory again concerning a few dates just before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the 16th and 17th of October, 2006. I'm referring to these interviews on page 20 in English, paragraph 109. Let me quote: [In English] " ... beginning of the war until 23rd July 1995, when I was transferred on the orders of Rajko Jankovic to the Intervention Platoon of the Semizovac Battalion." [Interpretation] Is this what you stated, Mr. Sejdic, and have I described the events in the right chronological order?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the way it was. From 1994 until 1995, I was with that man. I had to join him and his unit transferring from the Labour Platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Dutertre, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, you told us that until 1995, you worked in the Labour Platoon, then were transferred to the Intervention Platoon. This Intervention Platoon, is it a combat unit, a labour unit? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: It was not a labour unit. It was Ranko Jankovic's Intervention Platoon, and that was a special unit of his, and they went and launched attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us why you were transferred to this Intervention Platoon?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I will ask the same question again, or seemingly so. From the beginning of the war until you were transferred to this Intervention Platoon, did you work on a voluntary basis; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did your work on the Labour Platoon on the frontline and then your transfer to the Intervention Platoon, was this something that you did voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Paid?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So could you tell us why you did all this work and what made you do all this work?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, because that's what they demanded. I was captured there with my family, and they just said to me that I had no choice but to follow their orders and to do what they told me. And they said that if I tried to escape or anything else, my wife and children and parents would be in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "danger"? What did they mean by "danger"?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, if I tried to escape to my own side, the Muslim side, to become one of their soldiers or anything like that, they told me that I didn't even need to try that because they would kill my mother, father, wife, child, everything. That's how they threatened me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I will now try to briefly sum up the different events that you told us about, and you will tell me whether I understood what you told us correctly. Your village was attacked in April 1992, your village of Svrake.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor does not have the right to recapitulate in this way. It's up to him to question the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I disagree with you. The Prosecutor is fully allowed and entitled to review what the witness has just said and ask him whether what he has understood is correct. It's absolutely appropriate. You may ask questions after having reviewed the questions answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, the village of Svrake, your village, was attacked in April of 1992. The villagers put up some resistance for two to three days. Then you are sent to Srednje via Semizovac, through Semizovac. From Semizovac -- no, from Srednje, you're sent back to Semizovac. On the way to Semizovac, the two buses managed to slip away from their Serbian escort and managed to reach Korita, which was under Muslim control. You stay there some 20 days, and you are told that everything is quiet in Semizovac. And for this reason, you go back to Semizovac. On the way, you meet Mr. Spiric, who arrests your brother. Then you are forced to do chores for a couple days. Then, until 1995, you're forced to do labour within a work platoon first, and then you're transferred to Mr. Jankovic's Intervention Platoon. Have I summed things up correctly?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Rajko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Rajko Jankovic. Let's now return to some items that we have the background in mind, and let's go back to the attack on your village and what was happening right before. The first question: Were there any members of the SDS in Svrake before the village was attacked in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the local Serbs or the ones who came in ?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Local Serbs, members of your village.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you give us some names, names of the villagers from Svrake who were members of the SDS? Give us their names, please, so the Judges can know about this.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I won't be able to remember all of them, because it's been a long time, but roughly, Ilija Crnogorac, Nedjo Djukic, Nenad Boskovic. Then there was Zarko Mumalo, Blagoja Mumalo, and then there was Novo Divljanovic and Major Djukic, Cetko Jovicevic, Dragan Jeremic, Nenad Kuzmanovic, Jevto Vlahovic, Djukic, Jevto, or, rather, Jevto Djukic, Miro Kuzman, and the others. I can't remember any more names just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: People whose name you mentioned, are these people who lived in your own village or did they also live in surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Mostly from Semizovac, Israk [phoen] and Donja Vogosca, Srenjko [phoen]. Around Semizovac, basically, and Svrake. They were locals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I listened to what you said very carefully. You gave us a list of people who belonged to the SDS, but how did you know that they were members of the SDS, how can you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, they were people who were the main people when I was captured there. I know they were those locals, my former neighbours, as were -- and they would take us into custody and the other people, take us off to the prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but your answer raises new problems. You say that they escorted you when you were taken into custody, but one can conclude from this that the SDS was at the head of this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Serbs. Well, SDS, I don't know. What does "SDS" mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just said that you don't know what SDS is, but when you were answering Mr. Dutertre's question, he asked you, "Who were the members of the SDS," and you gave a list. So maybe there's a mistake here. This is where it comes from, this misunderstanding. When the question was put to you, you were asked -- you probably understood that you were asked the names of the people who arrested you and not the people who were members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were people who were mostly, from 1992 to the end of the war, were locals, my neighbours, those people who I knew, and I stated that those were the people and gave their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, you have the floor, but I believe there's a problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to shed some light on this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, do you know what is the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't know exactly what this means, this Democratic Party thing. All I know is that they were Serbs, quite simply, and I know these individual Serbs, the ones I knew. And I gave you their names, those who were the local villagers in my village, whom I knew very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The list of the people you mentioned is the list of the people who detained you at one point in time; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Not only me, but all the other people too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. First, the Prosecutor asked the witness who the members of the SDS were in Svrake, and the witness gave us some names. Then it was established that the witness does not know what the Serbian Democratic Party is, and then the Prosecutor says to him, "They were the people who detained you." And we saw how the situation evolved from what the witness previously said, and now the Prosecutor is putting something new to the witness that wasn't mentioned. The witness obviously mentioned the Serbs he knew by name. He didn't say that all those Serbs had incarcerated him. Maybe they did, but that's not what he said. So the Prosecutor cannot ask leading questions in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a leading question. This is what I recall from the French translation of the answer of the witness. Maybe the translation was faulty, maybe I misunderstood. I'm not going to make this a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, please, this list you gave us, is it the list of all the Serbs in your village, is it the list of the people who arrested you? Could you tell us exactly what this list corresponds to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: That is the list of names of people, Serbs, who were in my area, who were the main people at the time and responsible for the Muslim people. At the time, they exerted pressure on my local people, my Muslim neighbours, and they detained them, incarcerated them, took them away, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. When your village was attacked, could you tell us which units attacked the village? And I'm talking about April 1992.

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Our village was attacked by -- from Semizovac, from the direction of Krivoglavci, Donja Vogosca, and all the other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: If you know, could you tell us which units attacked? Was it the regular army, were they volunteers? Were you able to identify what these units were, since the attack went on for two to three days and then the attackers went into the village? So were you able to identify who the attackers were and the units?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, the attackers were the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Were there units of the Serbian army, regular army?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were in the barracks over there where the soldiers were, and they were with them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You saw these soldiers taking part in the attack? Did you eyewitness this or is it something that you heard later on?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: That was what I heard later. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor is once again asking a completely impermissible question. Until the 19th of May, the only regular army was the JNA, and along with it the Territorial Defence, so he can't ask if they were units of the regular Serb army. Where does he get the regular Serb army from? It's either the JNA or it was the Territorial Defence, or there were some units outside the JNA and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is May 19, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, April 1992. In April 1992 -- Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by the UN on May 22nd, 1992, unless I'm wrong. So normally at this moment in April, the army is the Army of the former Yugoslavia. The Prosecutor was putting questions to the witness to know exactly what he knew about the army, who was part of it, and which units were in the attack. I understood that you were try to elicit this from him, and he's saying "Serbs" as an answer. Maybe you can try and elicit this through other questions, maybe with the uniforms, the dress and so on. If you feel that maybe he's forgotten a number of things that he already had said in his statement, you can jog his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Sejdic, when the Serb attackers entered the village, your village, the first question: Could you tell us whether they were all dressed similarly; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, no, they weren't all dressed the same. Some wore the old type of army uniform. Others were dressed in civilian clothes or their own uniforms, just perhaps the top part would be one kind of uniform and the trousers something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you know the uniform of the JNA at the time of the attack, you knew what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the old type of uniform that was worn before the war in the army. I know what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Did you do your national service within the JNA? How long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are fully able to distinguish a JNA uniform, since you wore one, from another uniform that would not be a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wanted to ask this follow-up question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So soldiers entered into the village. Some were wearing JNA -- a JNA uniform. Can you tell us how the others were dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, they were dressed in black camouflage uniforms. They belonged to Rajko Jankovic, his men. They had special uniforms, black ones, and the rest wore army uniforms of the former army. So those who had them wore them, and they were the specials, mostly. Others who did not have any special uniform had military uniforms or the uniform of the former army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Among the people dressed in JNA uniform, did you see any officers?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't see any officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us where Rajko Jankovic comes from?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Rajko Jankovic is Semizovac, Vranjak village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Apart from these soldiers dressed in JNA uniforms and Rajko's men, Rajko Jankovic's men, did you notice any other soldiers that would belong to other units?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC
utterances.text: Well, they all wore the same clothes. From Vogosca and Ilijas, that area, from the direction of Semizovac, as they formed groups, they wore similar clothes, the old SMB olive-green-type uniform and the other military uniforms, except for the specials. The specials had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are talking about special units. Listening to you, I noted that some had black uniforms, so could you describe, if you remember, of course, how these people were dressed, what kind of gear they had with them? Could you give us some details? You said, yourself, these are special units, so how were they special? What made them different between them and those in SMB uniforms or those dressed in plainclothes? What was so special about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were young people, and they wore this special equipment. They wore those uniforms, and the older ones, the Serbs, the locals, that is, who were a little older, they wore the old type of uniform, those who hadn't been taking part in combat or any actions and so on. So the older people went to stand guard at the frontline, in the trenches, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that these were young people, but were they armed? And if they were armed, what kind of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they had automatic rifles, they had pistols, hand grenades, and they had jackets on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean flak-jackets or just jackets to be protected from the cold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vests or flak-jackets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they have anything on their faces or could you see nothing on their faces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of them had some sort of black paste and put it on their face or eyes, and they would have some bandanas 'round their heads, the younger ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small point of detail, but this could be of interest. These young people had black marks on their faces? You actually saw that? Are you quite sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many were there in that group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
